title: Algorithms and flowcharts
objectives: Say what an algorithm is, in simple English, and why a computer needs one.
List the usual properties of a good algorithm (clear steps, finite, definite).
Name the common flowchart symbols and what each one means.
Draw or read a flowchart for a sequence, a yes/no decision, and a simple repeat.
Dry-run (trace) a small algorithm with pencil values.
completionCriteria: Trace the tea-or-water algorithm with two different inputs without help.
Knowledge check score is complete; independent dry-run is correct.

notes.introduction: Before C, we write the plan. An algorithm is that plan in words or numbered steps. A flowchart is the same plan drawn with standard shapes.
notes.beginner: An algorithm is a finite list of clear steps that solve a problem. Anyone who follows the steps the same way should get the same kind of result. A flowchart is a picture of those steps. Ovals start and stop. Parallelograms show input or output. Rectangles show work. Diamonds ask a yes/no question. Arrows show what happens next.
notes.formal: An algorithm is a well-ordered, unambiguous, finite sequence of effective operations that produces a result and stops. A flowchart is a graphical representation of an algorithm using standard ISO-style teaching symbols (terminal, process, input/output, decision) connected by flow lines.

terms.meaning: A finite, clear sequence of steps to solve a problem.
A diagram of an algorithm using standard shapes and arrows.
Walking through the steps with sample values on paper.
A yes/no question that chooses the next path (diamond).
An arrow that goes back so a step can happen again until a condition changes.
Steps written in careful plain language that looks a bit like a program, but is not C yet.

revision: Oval = start/stop. Parallelogram = input/output. Rectangle = process. Diamond = decision.
Always dry-run with at least two sample inputs, including an awkward one.
notes.examAnswer: An algorithm is a finite set of unambiguous steps that solves a problem and then stops. A flowchart represents that algorithm: terminals (ovals), input/output (parallelograms), processes (rectangles), decisions (diamonds), connected by arrows. A dry run traces the arrows with sample data.

body.objectives: You should leave able to write numbered steps for a tiny everyday task and draw them with the four main shapes.
body.prerequisiteCheck: You already know a computer follows exact instructions (topic 1). If 'input' and 'memory' are still foggy, reopen that lesson. You still do not need C syntax.
body.introduction: A program is a translation of a plan. If the plan is messy, the program will be messy. This lesson trains the plan: algorithms and flowcharts. Unit 2 will turn decisions and repeats into C if, while, and for. Here we only draw them.
body.analogy: A recipe is an algorithm: a finite list of steps that, if followed, produces a dish. A flowchart is the same recipe drawn as boxes so you can see the forks: 'Is the water boiling? If no, wait; if yes, add tea.' You would not start cooking in a language you do not speak; you start with the recipe.
body.explanation:
An algorithm must be finite: it cannot tell the machine 'keep going forever' with no way out. It must be definite: each step means one thing. 'Add some sugar' is a poor step; 'add two spoons of sugar' is better. It must be effective: a person or a machine can actually do the step with the tools they have.

We write algorithms as numbered steps or as pseudocode. Example problem: a student is thirsty. Steps: (1) Start. (2) Ask: tea or water? (3) If tea, boil water, add tea, serve. (4) If water, pour water, serve. (5) Stop. That is already an algorithm. It has a start, a decision, two process paths, and a stop.

A flowchart uses a small set of shapes so another student (or an examiner) can read your logic quickly. The terminal oval marks Start and Stop. The parallelogram marks Read or Write (input/output). The rectangle marks work: add, set, compute. The diamond marks a question with two labelled ways out, usually Yes and No. Arrows are not decoration; they are the only legal order of steps.

A loop in a flowchart is not a new shape. It is an arrow that returns to an earlier box until a diamond says No (or Yes). Example: 'While the glass is empty, pour.' We mention this so a later for-loop in C does not appear from nowhere. We do not yet write C loops.

A dry run is how you check the drawing. Pick values. Write a tiny table: step, what is in the glass, what you do next. If the table never reaches Stop, the algorithm is wrong.
body.syntax: There is still no C. Pseudocode may look like: READ name / IF name is empty THEN write 'missing' / ELSE write 'hello'. That is teaching language, not a compiler language. Do not put semicolons and expect GCC to run it.

examples.title: Algorithm: larger of two numbers
steps: If A > B, write A as larger.
Stop. Dry run: A=3, B=10 → diamond is false → write 10.

examples.title: Flowchart with a repeat: fill a glass
steps: If No, process: pour a little, then arrow back to the decision.
This back-arrow is a loop in a flowchart. C while comes in Unit 2.

body.execution: Dry-run table for drink = water: Start → Read drink=water → tea? No → Pour water → Serve → Stop. For drink = tea: Start → Read tea → tea? Yes → Make tea → Serve → Stop. Both paths reach Stop. That is required.

trace.prompt: In the tea/water flowchart, if the input is water, which process box runs: Make tea or Pour water?

predict.prompt: An algorithm says: set n to 2; add 3 to n; write n. What number is written?

mistakes: Drawing arrows that never reach Stop — that is not a finished algorithm.
Putting two questions in one diamond. A teaching diamond is one yes/no question.
Using a fancy picture instead of the standard shapes. Examiners look for oval, parallelogram, rectangle, diamond.
Writing C code inside a flowchart box before you know C. Boxes hold short English actions.

guided.prompt: Name the four main flowchart shapes and what they stand for (start/stop, input/output, process, decision).

independent.prompt: Write a 5-step algorithm (not C) to decide whether a number n is zero or not, then say which step is the decision.

check.prompt: Which shape is used for a yes/no question?
An algorithm must be finite. What does that mean here?
Dry run: set x=4; if x>5 write BIG else write SMALL. What is written?

body.summary: An algorithm is a finite, clear plan. A flowchart draws that plan with standard symbols. Sequence, decision, and a returning arrow cover the logic you will later type as C. Always dry-run.
revision: Sketch the tea/water chart from memory.
Add one awkward input to any dry run (empty, zero, or 'neither').
